title: Skip the Hessian, Keep the Rates: Globalized Semismooth Newton with Lazy Hessian Updates
claim: Our second-order method converges an order of magnitude faster than the first-order baseline, and lazier Hessian updates still retain the speedup.
layout: 2 side-by-side log-log plots, shared legend on top, runtime vs epoch axes
description: Two side-by-side log-log line plots share a legend placed across the top. Both plots show gradient norm on the y-axis, falling from about 5 down to 1e-3. The left plot uses runtime in seconds on the x-axis and the right plot uses epoch count. The orange Adam curve decreases slowly. On the left it then oscillates wildly and blows up to large values. On the right it lags far behind the other curves. Several GLAd-SSN curves are shown: a purple one with no laziness, plus green, light blue, brown and pink for m=50, 100, 200 and 400. They drop much faster and reach 1e-3 to 1e-4. Lazier variants need more epochs but give similar or better wall-clock behavior. The eye goes first to the orange Adam curve and its noisy blow-up.
caption: Training neural networks with Lipschitz constraints (Section 5.1). GLAd-SSN performs an order of magnitude better than Adam in iteration count. Laziness (increasing m) helps significantly!
abstract: Second-order methods are provably faster than first-order methods, and their efficient implementations for large-scale optimization problems have attracted significant attention. Yet, optimization problems in ML often have nonsmooth derivatives, which makes the existing convergence rate theory of second-order methods inapplicable. In this paper, we propose a new semismooth Newton method (SSN) that enjoys both global convergence rates and asymptotic superlinear convergence without requiring second-order differentiability. Crucially, our method does not require (generalized) Hessians to be evaluated at each iteration but only periodically, and it reuses stale Hessians otherwise (i.e., it performs lazy Hessian updates), saving compute cost and often leading to significant speedups in time, whilst still maintaining strong global and local convergence rate guarantees. We develop our theory in an infinite-dimensional setting and illustrate it with numerical experiments on matrix factorization and neural networks with Lipschitz constraints.
